name: 2 Timothy
author: The letter names Paul as its writer, a Jewish teacher trained as a Pharisee (a strict keeper of Jewish law) and a tentmaker by trade, who became a travelling missionary and founded churches across the Roman world. Traditionally it is his last surviving letter, written from prison in Rome. Many scholars instead think a later follower wrote it in Paul's name, drawing on his memory and teaching, though many others hold to Paul himself.
audience: It is addressed to Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker for many years, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, apparently leading the church at Ephesus at the time. He faced rival teachers stirring up arguments, believers drifting away, and the danger that came with being linked to an imprisoned leader.
era: If written by Paul, it dates to around AD 64–67, under the emperor Nero, who blamed Christians for the great fire of Rome in AD 64 and had many put to death. Christianity was still a small, unofficial movement with no legal protection. Ephesus, a great port city in what is now western Turkey, was famous for its huge temple to the goddess Artemis. Those who think a follower wrote it usually place it some decades later.

notes.1:15: Asia here means the Roman province around Ephesus in western Turkey; Onesiphorus apparently came from Ephesus and searched Rome to find the imprisoned Paul.
notes.3:1: Jannes and Jambres are names Jewish tradition gave to Pharaoh's magicians who opposed Moses; the book of Exodus itself does not name them.
notes.3:10: Pisidian Antioch (not the larger Antioch in Syria), Iconium and Lystra were towns in south-central Turkey where Paul was attacked on his first missionary journey; Lystra was probably Timothy's hometown.
notes.4:6: Paul writes expecting execution soon; early church tradition holds that he was beheaded outside Rome during Nero's reign.
notes.4:9: The "first defence" probably means an initial hearing before a Roman court; Dalmatia was a region on the coast of modern Croatia.
notes.4:19: Priscilla and Aquila were a tentmaking married couple who had worked alongside Paul in Corinth and Ephesus years earlier.

flags.problem: 'Paul writes expecting execution soon' states Paul's authorship as settled, although the author section notes that many scholars think a later follower wrote the letter in his name.
flags.suggestion: Reword to follow the letter's own framing, e.g. 'The letter pictures Paul expecting execution soon; early church tradition holds that he was beheaded outside Rome during Nero's reign.'
